newsitem.title: INDIA: Bombay index falls 105 points, ends at day's low.
newsitem.headline: Bombay index falls 105 points, ends at day's low.

text.p: Shares at Bombay exchanges took a sharp fall on Wednesday, as financial year-end considerations played on the minds of major players, dealers said.
"People are squaring off outstanding positions ahead of the year-end," said Vijay Pandya, chief dealer at Classic Share & Stock Brokers.
"I don't think we need to press the alarm bells."

Lack of buying support led the Bombay Stock Exchange's (BSE) benchmark 30-share index to shed 104.78 points, or nearly three percent--the single largest fall since last month's pro-market budget unveiled by the government.
"To an extent, there is some bit of money tightening also. I think the entire market is just happier marked at lower levels," said Sanjeev Sanghvi, chief dealer at James Capel B&K.
The Bombay index leapt nearly 16 percent to an eight-month high of 4,029.56 from the pre-budget close of 3,474.79 before the rally ran out of steam.
"FIIs (foreign institutional investors) are waiting for the markets to cool," said Bharat Iyer, market strategist at UBS Securities, the investment arm of Union Bank of Switzerland.
"The markets are overbought. So a correction is underway," he said.
UBS's Iyer said good valuations would be the key factor luring foreign money into Indian stocks this year. "The budget has provided a strong impetus to kick start earnings," he said.
The 1997/98 (April-March) budget cut corporate and personal taxes, raised foreign portfolio limts in firms to 30 percent from 24 percent and allowed companies to buyback shares.
Share prices of Bayer India eased at the BSE despite higher profits of 103.30 million rupees in 1996 against 30 million in the previous nine-month period.
Bayer fell 50 rupees to 2,000 in low volume.
